beta_new: From the Maynard Burn (Tyler Peak) trailhead, a steep boot path climbs through rhododendron forest and past an old fire-break (the Maynard Burn track) to reach meadows and then the crest of Gray Wolf Ridge around 2.7 miles (~6,200 ft). Formal trail tread ends shortly after (~2.85 mi), and the final push to the summit is a cross-country scramble over a minor sub-summit and along the open ridge, arriving at Baldy's rocky, view-packed top at 3.6 miles. The route follows the Lower and Upper Maynard Burn Trail from the Maynard Burn (Tyler Peak) trailhead at the end of FR 2870-120, gaining a ridge crest via steep, sometimes faint tread through subalpine meadows and scree/talus to the Baldy summit block.

In October 1992 Peter Doorish's ascent of a route on the east face of Mount Baring, with Laura Woods, went at 5.10d, and he explicitly distinguished it from his other Baring-massif routes of that season by noting that all of them except the east face ascent were Grade V climbs of about fourteen pitches. That implies a shorter, lower-commitment line — probably Grade III or IV — but there is no recorded pitch count, no length, no topo and no description of the line itself. There is no evidence of a repeat ascent. Anyone going after it should treat it as an exploratory objective: identify the line from the ground, expect the same variable gneiss and vegetated ledges as the rest of the mountain, and be self-sufficient for retreat. The east side of Baring drops toward the upper Barclay Creek drainage and is not served by any climbers' path; the practical access is over or around the peak from the standard northwest-ridge approach, or up the east-side slopes from the Barclay Creek valley.

This line is also called the "South Scramble" (3rd class, Grade II) and the Northwest Ridge Route; they are the same line. From the Barclay Lake trailhead you do not follow the maintained lake trail — you take the abandoned logging road just uphill of it, find the cairned climbers' path at the first creek crossing, and go essentially straight up the forested west side. The path gains around 2,000 feet in about a mile to reach the ridge crest near 4,000 ft, follows the ridge east, drops below a cliff band, crosses a wooded gully and traverses into a boulder-filled basin at about 4,900 ft. From the basin, cross east and climb the obvious couloir/gully about 700 feet to the notch at roughly 5,550-5,600 ft between South Baring and the main peak. Turn north out of the notch, the angle eases, and easy class-3 scrambling on heather, talus and blocky gneiss leads a final quarter mile to the 6,127-ft north summit. Aim for the north summit — the south peak is lower and harder. The outing is rated Hard at 7.0 miles round trip with 3,500 ft of gain to a 6,129-ft high point; it is elsewhere described as closer to two miles one way with 3,700 ft of gain, or roughly 4,000 ft. The discrepancy is real and reflects different start points and how much of the logging-road walk is counted; either way the defining feature is gradient, not mileage.

The route involves four major vertical steps. The lower approach consists of approximately 2,300 feet of brush fighting up steep cliffs through dense vegetation (slide alder, vine maple, devil's club). The climbing involves vertical, delicate mixed terrain with roof sections requiring stirrup aid climbing on unusually hard rock (no specific rock type has been reliably sourced for this face) with poor natural protection. The crux is on the second step (400 feet) which features 120-degree roof sections and extremely delicate vertical climbing. On the lower brush sections, the first-ascent party fixed hundreds of feet of light ¼-inch rope hung from the brush to assist with load-hauling, with separate lengths of full-diameter climbing rope fixed at the most hazardous spots; double fixed ropes were placed specifically on the first step for hauling loads. Multiple attempts from 1951-1959 failed before the successful first ascent in 1960.

moves.from: Establish Dolomite Camp at the base of the first step.

value.name: Dolomite Camp
value.notes: Camp at the base of the first of the four vertical steps, after the brush-fighting approach.

beta_new: The most commonly climbed route on Bear Mountain's north face, established by Beckey and Fielding in 1967. The approach gains a glacier couloir on the west side of the north buttress. The upper buttress features seven roped pitches of excellent quality granitic rock with consistent protection. Route is usually climbed as a 2-3 day alpine adventure including a multi-day approach and descents.

From the Church Lake trailhead at the end of FS Road 3160, an easy but steep unofficial path climbs about 0.6 miles to Church Lake. From the lake the route continues around the shore and up through meadows toward a ridge/saddle above, then follows the ridge — which becomes steep but is 'nothing scary' — to a high point near peak 6066, with the final ~100 meters to the true summit requiring some class 3 scrambling on a narrow, occasionally exposed ridge. This is a hiker/scrambler route, not a roped climb; no technical gear is used on it.

From a camp near Dutch Miller Gap, ascend the left-hand of two parallel gullies on the SW Face (~1,000 ft, Class 3-4) to a ridge notch NW of the true summit, then climb the summit block in three short pitches (up to 5.6) to the top.

moves.from: Descend via three single-rope rappels and reverse the gully.

beta_new: The only documented ascent (Abegg's party, Aug 2012) climbed directly over the peak's east side and NW slopes rather than contouring around a subsidiary spur, finding mostly Class 3 terrain that is 'steep and mossy' with one or two unavoidable Class 4 moves; careful selection of moss and rock holds was needed on loose ground. Reported Day 1 stats for the full push from the road (including the Porkbelly Ridge approach and a descent to camp beyond the summit) were +6,550 ft / -1,820 ft over 6.3 miles — most of that gain occurs on the way to Berdeen's summit, with the loss coming afterward on the descent toward camp, so treat the raw numbers as slightly inclusive of travel past the summit rather than a pure car-to-summit figure.

The most commonly climbed and most-described line to the summit, but every source treats it as a serious, committing objective rather than a straightforward scramble; no route on Big Four is easy. Parties have turned back after finding natural avalanche activity in the couloir, and describe the final downclimb as frightening even for experienced climbers.

Big Four Mountain's first ascent came on July 19, 1931, when Forest Farr and Art Winder climbed the northwest ridge -- the original route to the summit. As with the mountain's other lines, this route begins from the Big Four viewpoint/ice caves trail approach on the Mountain Loop Highway.

First climbed March 2, 1996 by Bart Paull and Doug Littauer in a fast, ultralight, ~9-hour push with no bivy gear. The route starts up an 'ice ribbon' on the initial slabs (thin ice at roughly 65 degrees with a short 85-degree step), continues through the main couloir's three steps of mostly moderate terrain, and hits its crux about three-quarters height: a 100-foot pitch of nearly vertical ice, which gives way to steep, often runnelled snow. The upper section mixes rotten ice, shale, and drytooling moves up to roughly 95-degree angles before summit cornices, which may require tunneling through.

Starting from the Beckey-Tate approach, the route traverses sharply right over overlaps to a big ledge below an open-book corner. From there it climbs two classic, clean corner pitches — the second through a burly bulge at 5.11c, the route's crux — followed by a wide-crack section, then exits via easier cracks to the top of the wall.

Climbed ground-up over three days, the route forces its way through vertical-to-overhanging, crackless monolithic granite low on the wall via aid climbing through multiple roof systems ('the Kangaroofs'), protected by seven bolts on the first three pitches with bolted anchors. Above the roofs the route continues on natural gear to the top. The FA team topped out at 2 a.m. on August 19, 2012, bivied on the summit, and descended the next morning via the Beckey-Tate line.

This Grade II alpine route climbs about 200 feet of rock in three short pitches from the base of the summit block. The approach ascends parallel gullies on the west face of Kangaroo Ridge beneath Big Kangaroo. The route culminates in a steep, mostly unprotectable exposed 5.6 slab across the summit fin with a single rusty old bolt for protection.

From a roadside pullout on SR-20 east of Washington Pass, descend/cross Early Winters Creek and climb steeply up the Willow Creek drainage (brushy, staying on the north side) to about 5,000 ft where the grade eases. Continue up open basin terrain to roughly 7,000 ft, then cross a loose scree or snow slope (~400 ft) to gain the west ridge at a saddle near 7,400 ft. Follow the class 2 ridge crest to the base of the summit block, climb a short class 4/low-5th chimney/crack (about 50 ft) to a stance below the final slab, then make an unprotected 5.7-5.8 boulder move (often boosted via a shoulder stand) onto the roughly 20-ft summit friction slab and the true summit.

From the gated trailhead, walk or bike the old Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road roughly 7 miles to the unmarked boot path for Hardscrabble Lakes (near the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp). Climb past lower and upper Hardscrabble Lakes, staying close to the inlet to avoid cliff bands on climber's left. From upper Hardscrabble Lake, climb a gully to a col, drop onto the open granite slab of the north slope, then follow the east ridge to the summit.

From the Dingford Creek Trailhead, follow the maintained Dingford Creek Trail past the Hester Lake Trail junction to Myrtle Lake, then leave the trail and work steep, brushy terrain up to Big Snow Lake. Traverse right around Snowflake Lake and ascend chutes/rock ribs onto the upper mountain's rock fields; the final approach to the summit is class 2-3 scrambling. Serious route-finding and bushwhacking are required, and failed attempts due to losing the line are common.

Considered a quintessential North Cascades ridge climb. From Wing Lake camp, snow slopes (following the hogsback moraine wide right, then traversing back left) lead to a notch/col between the Northeast Ridge and neighboring Point 8995. Above the col the ridge is a straightforward but sustained climb: mostly 3rd and 4th class with a low-5th-class crux (commonly rated 5.2-5.4, with some parties finding a short 5.5-ish move near the top) about halfway up, plus a scramble past several loose towers low on the ridge that are typically bypassed on ledges just off the crest. Rock quality is poor low on the route and improves noticeably higher up. Most parties simul-climb much of the terrain and rope up only for the low-5th sections. First ascended by Roger Jackson and Michael Kennedy on September 1, 1973.

Two-pitch sport climb on a lower west-facing wall section of Keechelus Ridge. Can be climbed as one continuous pitch or split into two pitches using mid-route anchors. Described as one of the best 5.9s in Washington with commanding views from the belay stations. Belay ledge provides excellent sun protection during morning and midday hours.

Multiple independently-published trip reports (2006, 2013, 2023, and a winter ski ascent) describe the same standard line: gain the northeast ridge either from the Eureka Creek drainage to the north or from a col below the peak reached via Shellrock Basin/Shellrock Pass to the south, then follow class 2-3 talus, scree, and blocky black-hornfels terrain along the ridge crest to the summit. Sources explicitly note the route can be done without a rope, including in winter snow conditions. It is almost always climbed as part of a multi-day traverse with neighboring Mt. Lago, Mt. Carru, and/or Osceola Peak, since all share the same Shellrock Basin approach.

Extends the Sarcophagus line up the obvious straight-up headwall after the orange streak in the middle of the wall. Stand on the ledge boulder, clip two draws high, then start crimping through sustained climbing; holds improve near the final bolt. Two tactical options exist: carefully skip/back-clean certain bolts per a detailed clipping strategy to reduce rope drag, or take a ledge traverse and climb the extension directly off the ledge.

Steep start off a left-hand side-pull, placing a #1 Camalot into a pod before clipping into bolted protection; a rest ledge partway up breaks the pitch before a pumpy, sustained bolted sequence moving left and up to the anchor.

First ascended by Eric Wehrly and Sam Boyce in August 2023. Grade V, 5.10+, 16 pitches, with just over 2,000 ft of net elevation gain and about 2,800 ft of total climbing distance on the west face of the Southwest Summit (9,320'). The route sits 'looker's right' of its established neighbors, the Soviet and Oregonian routes. A weathered, decades-old cam found at pitch 4 suggests a prior abandoned attempt on similar terrain.

From Holden basecamp (Holden Lake or Holden Pass), approach via established trail to glacier base at ~7,300 ft. Rope up and ascend Mary Green Glacier bearing west along its north edge, then traverse southwest to the glacier's upper corner. Climb the steep upper snow finger to the right until reaching rock; transition to the northeast ridge with mostly Class 3-4 rock just right of a gully for several rope lengths, then traverse left to a prominent notch in the upper ridge north of summit. Scramble Class 4 loose ridge crest past large blocks to the summit horn.

From the buttress base (~8,350 ft), the ridge steepens and narrows quickly. Climbing is mostly solid rock but lichen-covered in places, with sustained sections in the 5.7 range and sections of wild exposure along the crest. Expect roughly 4 hours of climbing from the buttress base to Bonanza's true (main) summit.

First ascended by Seth Keena and Erik Bonnett in early September 2013 (ascent dated 9/4/2013). Rated V, 5.9+, 2,200 ft total: 1,600 ft of new terrain (mostly sustained 5.6-5.8 with moves to 5.9+, via ramp/ledge systems) then 600 ft shared with the Soviet Route to the summit. It begins a few hundred yards left of the Soviet Route, making the Soviet and Oregonian the two established lines on this northwest wall. The first-ascent team's approach that year was an unusually long ~32-mile one-way trip (including ~10 miles of biking) due to ferry/road closures in effect at the time - this is not the standard approach.

From a camp near the head of Park Creek, climb easier cliffs to a small glacier at the base of the face, then go left up the glacier to an icefall and traverse right through and under it (reported as a genuinely exposed, 'frightening' crossing) to reach the main rock wall. Follow a prominent central rib essentially straight up the face on generally sound Cascade granodiorite/orthogneiss, through a crumbly red rock stratum that crosses the whole face at roughly mid-height, to a 100-foot notch near the summit, then on to the top. The face averages about 70 degrees and is over 3,000 feet high.

From a camp at or near Park Creek Pass, ascend toward the Booker-Buckner col, crossing a broad sandy gully around 6,900 ft roughly a mile from the pass; a few crevasses/cracks near the col are typically bypassed on snowbridges. From the col, the northwest side of Booker is mostly Class 3 scrambling with some easy Class 2-3 terrain to the summit.

Most parties combine Booker with Buckner Mountain in the same trip since both share the Cascade Pass/Sahale Arm approach and the Horseshoe Basin traverse. From Sahale Camp/Sahale Arm, descend Sahale's south side to a snow-free gully near 6,600 ft into Horseshoe Basin, traverse (staying roughly 6,400-6,600 ft) past the Buckner buttress, then follow a north-facing rock gully and permanent snowfield (7,000-7,200 ft) to the south-trending ridge west of Booker's summit. Finish up talus, slabs, and a short, somewhat exposed 3rd-class (locally 4th-class-step) gully/dike to the summit. Routefinding through Horseshoe Basin is the crux of the day, not the climbing itself.

Climbs steep, sometimes hollow-feeling ice (P1, WI5) into a corner of excellent ice (P2, WI4), a gully approach beneath a hanging dagger (P3, WI3), a technical M7/WI4 crux pitch through overhanging rock with thin gear (P4), a blue-ice traverse (P5, WI4), and a long steep snow/ice headwall (roughly 45-60 degrees with vertical ice steps) to the summit ridge.

The standard approach ascends unroped via ledges on the east/southeast face to minimize rockfall danger. Parties typically establish camps at Boston Basin low camp (5,300 ft) or high camp (6,400 ft), then traverse via the Boston-Sahale saddle to access the summit route. Most ascents run roughly 10-11 hours from high camp to summit and back, per the detailed schedule.

moves.from: Rope is essential for descent via three rappel stations.

beta_new: The route begins below the west face and climbs steep snow heading NE for two pitches (belays under a bulge, then where a gully opens to the east), then follows a large gully east on pitch 3 (occasional rock hooks in the snow), continues up on pitch 4 to about 200 ft north of the summit, and finishes on pitch 5 across an exposed ridge to the true summit after a short rock step. A winter ascent found steep snow that grew icier and more rime-choked toward the north ridge, stayed on snow rather than take the harder mixed direct gully, and needed significant rime-ice removal to find gear and a bergschrund circumvented by climbing to climber's right.

Climb the first three pitches of the Southwest Rib, then go left at a ledge. A short, loose 5.2 pitch leads to a belay below the roofs; the money pitch pulls under and over double roofs at 5.10b with good gear, followed by an easy chimney into 5.9 thin hands to a ledge with great position, joining the upper Southwest Rib/South Arete descent.

Ground-up bolted route established by Brenden Sullivan and Jim Yoder up a network of gullies on the southern flank; 4 pitches of easy-to-moderate climbing (5.2–5.6) on knobby, cobble-studded welded-tuff breccia, finishing through a band of basalt to a low-angle summit chute shared with Cobbles 101.

The usual way up comes from the west, which means a long way round even though the peak stands only about three miles from Trinity. From the Trinity Trailhead, the Buck Creek Trail (#1513) climbs about 9.6 miles and 3,100 ft to Buck Creek Pass. From the pass an unmaintained high route winds around the west side of Liberty Cap and south to High Pass; contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, climb a short Class 3 step onto the ridge just south of Point 7839, and walk down into Louis Creek Basin to camp. From the basin, broad pumice, talus and low-angle snow lead up the broad west shoulder toward the top, and loose, slabby schist with one short Class 3-4 step near a horn goes to the summit. Some parties come in over Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valley instead. A direct line from King Lake on the east side exists but is brushy, involves a river ford, and is seldom used.

From the Upper Big Quilcene Trailhead, Trail #833 climbs through old-growth forest past Shelter Rock Camp and Camp Mystery to the open alpine gap of Marmot Pass (~6,000 ft), one of the most scenic passes in the Olympics. From the pass, turn right onto the Tubal Cain Trail and follow it north about 100 m to a junction, then leave it and climb right up switchbacks along the ridge, over a minor ~6,800 ft knob, to Buckhorn's southwest summit (6,988 ft) — the higher of its two nearly-equal summits. The final approach is loose scree, not quite Class 3, finishing with a short scramble onto a large summit boulder. When snow-free, the route requires no technical gear or roped travel.

From Sahale Glacier Camp at 7,600 feet, descend the south ridge of Sahale Peak to Horseshoe Basin. Traverse across snowfields approximately 2 miles to the mountain's base. Ascend steep snowfields with the distinctive cow-skull-shaped snowfield as a navigational landmark. The climb involves navigating steepening snow chutes and slopes at 35-40 degrees. The final 100 feet is Class 2-3 rock scrambling to the summit block. Total route elevation gain from camp is approximately 3,000 feet.

From Bullseye Pass (~6,200 ft), parties drop packs and climb the steep southeast slope on foot/hands to grippy granite, working up and over a hump before dropping beneath the summit on its western side (Class 3 traverse). The final approach to the true summit follows the south ridge and requires roped Class 4-5.0 climbing — two independent accounts describe one to two short pitches on excellent, hold-covered granite, finishing with an exposed high step onto a one-person summit perch.

This is considered the standard and easiest route up Burgundy Spire. Recommended for climbers experienced in alpine rock and comfortable with route-finding on exposed terrain. The route features many traverses, down-climbs, and loose features that demand careful attention.

moves.from: Descent is accomplished via 5 double-rope rappels down the middle of the upper face.

beta_new: This is the peak's standard (easiest) route, reached from the Dutch Miller Gap Trail. After a long approach and a cold river ford, parties climb through brush and talus on the peak's north side to about 5,400 ft, then ascend a gully (reported as a northeast gully) that holds a steep snow ramp and a moat into mid-summer, before boulder-hopping the final talus to the summit. It is described as seldom visited, with real route-finding and bushwhacking involved; a neighboring northwest gully is reported to involve Class 4 terrain and should be avoided.
